wait, OpenAI just built an AI system that found 948 distinct vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel that could let someone with limited access gain full control of a machine.

and it didn't just find bugs. it tested them, built working exploits, and even generated possible fixes.

all in one run costing around $1.2M in API credits.

i went through the full research article because those numbers sounded insane, but honestly, what they actually built is even more interesting.

here's what happened 👇

Linux is basically everywhere. cloud servers, Android devices, supercomputers, and a huge part of the internet rely on it.

at its core is the Linux kernel, which manages things like memory, hardware, and system permissions.

now imagine someone already has basic access to a machine, but a bug lets them gain full administrator control (root access).

that's called local privilege escalation (LPE).

finding these bugs usually takes skilled security researchers a lot of time. they have to read through massive amounts of code, test different ideas, and prove whether something can actually be exploited.

so OpenAI basically built a team of AI agents to automate much of that process.

one group searched the kernel for security-sensitive code. another examined it for possible vulnerabilities.

then other agents tested those findings inside isolated virtual machines. they'd run a test, check the results, adjust their approach, and try again.

once a bug was confirmed, another group checked whether it could actually be exploited to gain root access.

finally, the AI generated candidate patches for human researchers to review before reporting the findings to Linux maintainers.

so it wasn't just AI reading code and saying "hey, this looks vulnerable."

it was investigating, experimenting, learning from failures, proving security impact, and suggesting fixes.

basically, a huge part of what a security research team normally does, connected into one automated process.

and the results were pretty wild.

out of 2,308 potential findings, the system reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed 1,169 working privilege escalation exploit instances covering 948 distinct vulnerabilities.

plus 291 working information leak proofs of concept.

and these exploits worked on a stock Linux desktop configuration with standard security protections enabled, not some intentionally weakened machine.

the total cost? about $1.21M in API credits, or roughly $1,279 per distinct LPE vulnerability.

for perspective, hacking competitions have historically offered $20k–$70k for certain Linux kernel exploits.

using those rates, OpenAI estimated a hypothetical value of $18.9M–$66.3M.

obviously not actual earnings or guaranteed rewards, but it shows how much the economics of security research could change.

and one detail genuinely caught me off guard.

while reviewing a sample of exploits, researchers found at least 10 exploitation techniques that even the outside security experts OpenAI consulted hadn't seen before.

so the agents weren't just applying known tricks. they were experimenting and finding approaches that appeared new even to experienced researchers.

another interesting part is how quickly these capabilities seem to be improving.

in July, an earlier OpenAI model found and exploited 166 distinct Linux privilege escalation vulnerabilities.

in October, their upcoming cyber model found 948.

different scans, so not a perfect comparison, but still a pretty significant jump in just a few months.

now think about what this could mean.

Linux maintainers and security researchers are constantly trying to secure software that billions of people indirectly rely on.

if AI can handle much of the investigation, security teams could discover serious bugs earlier, verify them faster, and prepare fixes before attackers take advantage.

companies could audit their software more regularly, and the same approach could eventually help secure browsers, libraries, and other critical software too.

but there's a catch.

finding 948 vulnerabilities doesn't mean they're all fixed. OpenAI says they've already sent hundreds of reports and patches, but maintainers still need to review, test, and accept the fixes.

also, these are LOCAL privilege escalation vulnerabilities. it doesn't mean anyone can remotely hack every Linux machine.

and the AI wasn't perfect either.

during an earlier experiment, researchers discovered that 20 supposedly successful exploits had actually gained root access through a different vulnerability than the one the agents were supposed to test.

the AI got the result, but for the wrong reason.

so OpenAI added extra checks to verify how the agents actually achieved their results.

that part stuck with me because it shows why human oversight and independent verification still matter.

and there's another side to all this.

if AI makes finding vulnerabilities faster and cheaper for defenders, similar capabilities could make things easier for attackers too.

which means finding bugs earlier is only half the problem. fixing them quickly matters just as much.

and i think that's my biggest takeaway from the article.

it's not really about the 948 vulnerabilities or the $1.2M.

it's that we're moving from AI helping researchers with individual tasks to AI agents handling huge parts of an actual security investigation.

reading code, testing ideas, learning from failures, proving vulnerabilities, and proposing fixes. all in one automated workflow, with humans reviewing the results.

and this is still a research prototype.

imagine what happens as models get more capable and cheaper to run. we could potentially have systems constantly finding weaknesses in the software we rely on.

which sounds great, until you realize attackers could benefit from the same progress.

so the question i keep coming back to is this.

what happens when finding serious security bugs becomes easier than fixing them?

because if AI can discover vulnerabilities at this scale, we're going to need equally capable systems to verify and patch them.

otherwise, we'll just get much better at finding problems we can't fix fast enough.

and that's what makes this research both exciting and a little scary to me.

⚠️ 🇨🇦 🧠 Carney’s $1.6-Billion Cohere Stake Faces Reality Check as Models Rank Near 210th on Arena at 1354 Elo

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s claim that Canadians will own a piece of Cohere’s “world-leading secure AI” is marketing language that independent human-preference rankings have already disproven, with the firm’s strongest model at roughly 1354 Elo and near 210th overall.

On October 29, 2026, the federal government announced an equity investment of up to $1.6 billion in Toronto-based Cohere as part of a financing round targeting roughly $7 billion and a post-money valuation near $35.7 billion. The official release described the move as giving Canadians a stake in “secure, sovereign AI” built in Canada, with commitments that the company remain headquartered in the country and invest at least $1.7 billion in domestic computing infrastructure by 2030. Carney’s accompanying post on X repeated the “world-leading” framing.

The numbers on the LMSYS Chatbot Arena, the most widely cited blind human-preference ranking, tell a different story. As of late October 2026 snapshots, Cohere’s strongest listed model, Command A (03-2025), sits at approximately 1354 Elo. That places the lab around 23rd or 24th among roughly 28 providers and the model itself near 209th to 215th overall. Leading systems from Anthropic and Google routinely score above 1500, with gaps of 150 points or more that reflect clear differences in user preference on open-ended tasks.

Even within enterprise-focused or open-weight categories, Command A does not dominate. Aggregators show it lagging frontier proprietary models on agentic, coding, and knowledge work while remaining competitive mainly on cost or deployment constraints. Other Cohere variants rank still lower. By contrast, systems developed by xAI, including Grok variants, appear in the mid-to-high 1470s on the same Arena boards—materially closer to the current frontier without requiring a multi-billion-dollar government equity injection to declare national leadership.

Sovereign Super Intelligence capacity is a legitimate strategic objective. Data residency, controlled deployments, and reduced dependence on a handful of foreign providers matter for governments and regulated industries. Cohere has focused on private deployments and regulated sectors, which is a real commercial niche. That niche, however, is not the same as frontier capability. Equating a mid-tier provider with “world-leading” status requires the public to ignore the ranking data that every other serious lab tracks daily.

The investment also illustrates the recurring risk of industrial policy that picks winners with taxpayer capital. The round includes private participants such as Nvidia and Schwarz Group; the government’s stake is staged and commercial on paper. Yet the accompanying rhetoric treats the equity purchase as proof of technological sovereignty rather than a concentrated bet on one firm whose public benchmarks have not kept pace with the leaders. History in this sector shows that capability gaps are closed by research velocity and compute scale, not by press releases.

Canadians can reasonably want domestic Super Intelligence options that protect sensitive data and keep economic upside at home. Those goals are better served by accurate measurement of what the technology actually delivers than by promotional language that independent rankings contradict. The Arena numbers are public, updated, and based on millions of blind votes. They remain the clearest available check on claims of world leadership.

Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Small, scoring 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index - their plan to release its weights would make it the highest-scoring open weights model developed outside China based on current rankings

Inkling 2 Small is launching as a proprietary model, available first-party through @thinkymachines' Tinker platform and Tinker Playground, with weights to be released at a later date. Its score is up 18 points from Inkling Small, with ~4x as many output tokens per task. It matches @GoogleDeepMind's Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) and surpasses @XiaomiMiMo's MiMo-V2.6-Pro on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0.1.

Key takeaways:

➤ Large gains over Inkling Small, especially on agentic tasks: AutomationBench-AA rises from 5% to 46% and FrontierCode 2.0 from 5% to 25%. HLE-Diamond also rises from 12% to 29%.

➤ Different coding strengths from Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium): Inkling 2 Small scores 25% on FrontierCode 2.0 vs. 11% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium), but 13% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 vs. 30%.

➤ Creative agentic scores above Claude Haiku 5.5 and Grok 4.7 on AA-3D: Inkling 2 Small also scores above Gemini 3.8 Flash on both AA-3D and Code2Video-AA, but behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 on both.

➤ Research-level physics improves, but trails Gemini 3.8 Flash (high): Inkling 2 Small scores 56% on CritPt v2, up from 34% for Inkling Small, vs. 65% for Gemini 3.8 Flash (high).

➤ Fewer hallucinations from more selective answering: On AA-Omniscience v1.1, the hallucination rate falls from Inkling Small's 61% to 27%, while accuracy rises from 32% to 34% and the attempt rate falls from 77% to 53%.

➤ ~4x as many output tokens: Inkling 2 Small averages ~150K output tokens per Intelligence Index task vs. ~37K for Inkling Small, ~31K for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium), and ~99K for Gemini 3.8 Flash (high).

➤ Almost 6x the cost of Inkling Small, but cheaper than several other models with similar Intelligence Index scores: Inkling 2 Small costs $1.18 per Intelligence Index task vs. $0.20 for Inkling Small, $7.77 for Gemini 3.8 Flash (high), and $10.02 for Claude Sonnet 5.5 (medium).

Key model details:

➤ Type: Proprietary reasoning model at launch; Apache 2.0 weights release planned (date unconfirmed)

➤ Modalities: Text and image input, text output

➤ Size: 594B total parameters / 17B active parameters

➤ Pricing: $0.30/$1.00 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.03 per 1M cached input tokens)

➤ Availability at launch: Tinker and Tinker Playground

Congratulations to the team at @thinkymachines on the release!
